summary: The web address of the page is forwarded to Sentry exactly as it is, and the part after the '#' is never hidden — but that is precisely where the subscriber's secret management key sits while they are on the manage page, so a browser error report from that page can carry the key out of the building.
requires: a deployment with the Sentry DSN set (production or preview)

a browser-side event captured while the visitor is still on the manage page with the secret in the address — most durably after a render or hydration error, because the code that strips the secret from the address lives in an effect that a failed render never reaches
evidence: scrubEvent rebuilds the request block as {url, method, query_string} and passes both strings through redactText, which only rewrites email addresses, 'scheme://user:pass@' credentials, and '?key='/'&token=' style query parameters. A '#<secret>' suffix has no rule, and a bare 'token=...' in query_string cannot match either because the pattern requires a leading '?' or '&'. On the browser side the SDK's default HttpContext integration fills request.url from document.location.href, fragment included, and the manage link delivers its key as that fragment (manage-token-bridge.tsx reads location.hash). Suggested fix: reduce the URL to origin plus pathname before it leaves, or add a fragment rule to redactText, and cover it with a case in sentry-options.test.ts.

summary: The 'something went wrong' screen asks Sentry to record the error, but nothing has switched Sentry on at that moment, so the report is quietly dropped — losing exactly the browser errors these screens exist to report.
requires: a client-side render or hydration error
the error happening before the deferred start-up that only runs after the page's load event and an idle callback
evidence: instrumentation-client.ts calls startSentryClient() only inside loadSentry(), which is scheduled from a 'load' listener plus requestIdleCallback. app/error.tsx (line 23) and app/global-error.tsx (line 19) import the same module but never trigger that start-up, and the SDK's captureException returns silently when no client has been initialised on the scope. A first-paint hydration error therefore races the load event and is often lost with no signal. Suggested fix: export a single report helper from src/config/sentry-client.ts that starts the client if it is not running, and have both boundaries call that instead of captureException directly.

summary: Three cleaning steps are installed for errors, traces and log lines, but not for the standalone performance measurements the browser sends on their own, so if browser performance tracking is ever switched on those would leave uncleaned.
requires: NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_BROWSER_TRACES_SAMPLE_RATE set, which the runbook describes as a supported future step
evidence: sharedOptions sets beforeSend, beforeSendTransaction and beforeSendLog but no beforeSendSpan. In the pinned SDK, standalone spans (the browser's web-vital measurements) are packaged by createSpanEnvelope, which consults only beforeSendSpan and ignoreSpans — neither beforeSend nor beforeSendTransaction runs on them, and the HttpContext integration puts the page's full address on segment spans. Suggested fix: add a beforeSendSpan that runs the same scrubber, so the promise of a single choke point holds when tracing is enabled.

summary: The '/monitoring' address the browser reports through is an open, unauthenticated forwarder: anyone can post anything through the site's own domain to any Sentry account, at the site's expense.
requires: a deployed site (the forwarder only exists once the build plugin adds its rewrite)
evidence: tunnelRoute: '/monitoring' makes the build plugin add a Next.js rewrite whose destination interpolates the organisation and project identifiers straight from the request's own query parameters, with no check that they are this project's. Every such request is a billed invocation and egress on the site's account, which the threat model lists as in scope for abusive public traffic. Suggested fix: note the accepted risk in the runbook, or gate the path (rate limit or firewall rule) the way the other public entry points are treated.

summary: A comment tells the next reader that a particular test guards the nightly job's schedule, but no test by that name exists — the real check lives somewhere else.
evidence: The header comment names tests/unit/maintenance-monitor-config.test.ts; that file is not in the repository, and the assertion that the monitor's schedule equals the one in vercel.json actually lives in app/api/cron/maintenance/route.test.ts. Suggested fix: point the comment at the real file so the 'change both or neither' instruction stays followable.
